questions.question: How does the MongoDB aggregation pipeline work, and how do you use $match, $group, and $lookup stages in a Java application?
questions.title: MongoDB Aggregation Pipeline: $match, $group, $lookup
questions.direct_answer: The **aggregation pipeline** is a sequence of stages that transform documents as they flow through — Unix pipes for BSON. **`$match`** filters early (use indexes when it's the first stage). **`$group`** collapses documents by an `_id` expression with accumulators like `$sum`, `$avg`, `$push`, `$addToSet`. **`$lookup`** performs a left-outer join against another collection, producing an array that `$unwind` flattens for 1:1 matches. **`$project` / `$addFields`** reshape output. In Spring Data MongoDB you compose pipelines with the fluent `Aggregation` builder (`match`, `group`, `lookup`, `unwind`, `project`) executed via `MongoTemplate.aggregate()`. **Pipeline order drives performance** — reduce cardinality early; large sorts and groups need `allowDiskUse(true)` past 100MB.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to compose non-trivial server-side aggregations and understand stage ordering for performance
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Placing `$match` after `$group`/`$lookup`, forgetting to `$unwind` after `$lookup`, or pulling documents to Java to aggregate in memory
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name the 100MB sort spill, mention `allowDiskUse`, `$facet` for parallel pipelines, and `$merge` / `$out` for materialized-view output

sections.title: The Pipeline Mental Model
sections.content:
The MongoDB aggregation pipeline is a sequence of **stages**, each a function from a stream of documents to a stream of documents. Documents flow in one end; a transformed stream comes out the other. Each stage is independent and composable — just like Unix pipes for structured data.

The aggregation framework is MongoDB's answer to SQL's `GROUP BY`, `JOIN`, and window functions.
- The common core stages are **`$match`** (filter), **`$project`/`$addFields`** (reshape), **`$group`** (aggregate), **`$lookup`** (join), **`$unwind`** (flatten array), and **`$sort`/`$limit`/`$skip`** (ordering and pagination).
- More advanced stages include **`$facet`** (run multiple pipelines in parallel), **`$bucket`** (histograms), **`$graphLookup`** (recursive joins), and **`$merge`/`$out`** (write results back).

**Order matters** — a `$match` at the start can use an index to skip entire segments of the collection; the same `$match` after a `$group` runs against the full grouped output. Push filters, projections, and limits as early as possible.

sections.title: Pipeline Stage Flow
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    coll["orders collection"] --> match["$match: status, date"]
    match --> group["$group: by customerId, sum total"]
    group --> lookup["$lookup: customers"]
    lookup --> unwind["$unwind: customer"]
    unwind --> project["$project: reshape fields"]
    project --> sort["$sort: total desc"]
    sort --> limit["$limit: 10"]
    limit --> out["Result stream"]
```

sections.title: `$match` — Filter Early with Indexes
`$group` — Aggregate with Accumulators
sections.content:
**Common accumulators**
- `$sum`, `$avg`, `$min`, `$max` — numeric aggregates
- `$push` — collect into array (preserves duplicates)
- `$addToSet` — collect unique values
- `$first`, `$last` — first/last value in group order
- `$count` (4.4+) — simpler than `$sum: 1`

```javascript
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { status: "SHIPPED" } },
  { $group: {
      _id: "$customerId",
      orderCount: { $sum: 1 },
      totalSpent: { $sum: "$totalCents" },
      avgBasket:  { $avg: "$totalCents" },
      lastOrderAt:{ $max: "$createdAt" },
      skus:       { $addToSet: "$items.sku" }
  }}
]);
```

**Spring Data Java**

```java
GroupOperation group = Aggregation.group("customerId")
    .count().as("orderCount")
    .sum("totalCents").as("totalSpent")
    .avg("totalCents").as("avgBasket")
    .max("createdAt").as("lastOrderAt");
```

sections.title: `$lookup` — Server-Side Joins
Assembling in Spring Data
Performance Considerations
sections.content:
**When pipelines help:**
- Server-side aggregation avoids shipping raw documents over the wire
- `$match` first uses indexes
- `$merge` / `$out` materialize results for reuse

**When they hurt:**
- `$lookup` without an index on the foreign key — full-collection scan per input doc
- Large `$group` without `allowDiskUse` blows past the 100MB limit
- `$lookup` on sharded collections has historical constraints (check version)

**Watch for:**
- Stage ordering — always `$match` → `$project` → heavy stages
- `$unwind` after `$lookup` for 1:1 joins
- `$facet` for parallel sub-pipelines in one pass
- `$merge` beats `$out` for incremental materialization

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Pipeline = stream of stages**; each transforms the document stream
- **`$match` first** to use indexes and shrink the set
- **`$group`** with accumulators — `$sum`, `$avg`, `$push`, `$addToSet`
- **`$lookup` + `$unwind`** is the canonical join shape
- **Sub-pipeline `$lookup`** lets you filter/project inside the join
- **`allowDiskUse(true)`** for pipelines exceeding 100MB memory
- **`$merge` / `$out`** materialize results back into a collection

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Frame the pipeline**
- Sequence of stages; documents stream through
- Each stage is a function from stream to stream

**Cover the core stages**
- `$match` first — uses indexes
- `$group` — collapses by `_id` with accumulators
- `$lookup` — left-outer join, result arrives as array, `$unwind` flattens
- `$project`/`$addFields` — reshape output

**Emphasize ordering**
- Reduce cardinality early
- Heavy stages last on smallest possible input

**Mention the operational realities**
- `allowDiskUse(true)` for large pipelines
- `$merge` / `$out` for materialized views
- Indexes on foreign fields for `$lookup`

**Close with the Spring Data builder**
- `Aggregation.newAggregation(match, group, lookup, unwind, project, sort, limit)`
- Executed via `mongoTemplate.aggregate()`

questions.question: How does MongoDB support multi-document ACID transactions, and what are the limitations you should be aware of?
questions.title: MongoDB Multi-Document ACID Transactions
questions.direct_answer: Since **MongoDB 4.0 (replica sets)** and **4.2 (sharded clusters)**, multi-document transactions deliver ACID across documents and collections. They use **snapshot isolation** and **MVCC**; reads inside the transaction see a consistent snapshot from the moment it started, and conflicting concurrent writes raise `WriteConflict` and must retry. In Spring Boot you register a **`MongoTransactionManager`** bean and annotate service methods with **`@Transactional`**. The realities: transactions require a replica set (not standalone), have a default **60-second timeout**, add WiredTiger cache pressure, and should be used only when cross-document atomicity is genuinely required — single-document writes are always atomic natively.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding when MongoDB transactions are genuinely needed and the operational cost of using them
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using transactions for every write, or attempting them on a standalone `mongod`
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention MVCC snapshot isolation, `withTransaction` retry loop on `TransientTransactionError`, the 60s limit, and sharded cluster two-phase commit cost

sections.title: Why and When
sections.content:
Before 4.0, MongoDB offered only **single-document atomicity** — and that's still the default.
- Embedded arrays, nested subdocuments, and multi-field updates on one document are atomic without a transaction and without the overhead.
- The guidance is: **design for single-document atomicity first**; use transactions only when cross-document invariants truly require it.

When you do need them, MongoDB transactions provide **full ACID**: atomic commit, consistent snapshot reads, snapshot isolation between concurrent transactions, and durable replication.
- Under the hood they rely on **MVCC** — writes inside a transaction create versioned snapshots; concurrent transactions touching the same document raise `WriteConflict` and must retry.
- On sharded clusters, the cluster coordinates **two-phase commit** across shards, paying a latency tax for cross-shard atomicity.

sections.title: Using `withTransaction` from the Driver
Spring Boot with `MongoTransactionManager`
Replica Set vs Sharded Cluster Transactions
sections.content:
| Aspect | Replica Set (4.0+) | Sharded Cluster (4.2+) |
|---|---|---|
| Scope | Multiple docs, multiple collections in one DB/replica set | Docs across shards |
| Coordination | Primary commits | Two-phase commit coordinator |
| Latency | Low | Higher — round-trips to shards |
| Max duration | 60s default (`transactionLifetimeLimitSeconds`) | Same |
| Write concern | `majority` recommended | `majority` required |
| Typical use | Cross-collection invariants | Unavoidable cross-shard writes |

sections.title: When to Reach for a Transaction
sections.content:
**When they help:**
- True cross-document/cross-collection invariants (transfer, reserve + charge)
- Multi-step workflows that must all succeed

**When they hurt:**
- Single-document writes — use atomic updates instead
- Hot paths — transactions add WiredTiger cache pressure
- Long-running operations inside a transaction — blocks replication

**Watch for:**
- **60s lifetime limit** — long transactions auto-abort
- **Standalone mongod** can't use transactions — need replica set
- **Oplog pressure** on high-rate transactional writes
- **`TransientTransactionError`** signals a retryable abort — wrap with retry
- Prefer designing the schema so single-document atomicity covers the invariant (embed small aggregates, use subset pattern)

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Available since 4.0** on replica sets, **4.2+** on sharded clusters
- **Snapshot isolation via MVCC**; conflicting writes raise `WriteConflict`
- **`withTransaction`** retries `TransientTransactionError` automatically
- **Spring `@Transactional`** needs a `MongoTransactionManager` bean
- **Single-document atomicity** covers most needs — use transactions sparingly
- **60-second timeout** by default; long transactions auto-abort
- **`writeConcern: majority`** recommended (required on sharded)

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**State the capability**
- MongoDB supports multi-document ACID since 4.0 (replica set) and 4.2 (sharded cluster)
- Snapshot isolation via MVCC

**Give the Spring recipe**
- Register `MongoTransactionManager` bean
- Use `@Transactional` on service methods
- Requires replica set — standalone mongod won't work

**Show the driver idiom**
- `session.withTransaction(...)` auto-retries transient errors
- Read concern `snapshot`, write concern `majority`

**Close with the discipline**
- Single-doc writes are atomic natively — don't wrap every write
- 60s timeout; keep transactions short
- Sharded transactions use 2PC — more expensive; design to avoid

questions.question: How do you diagnose and optimize slow queries in MongoDB using `explain()` and other performance tools?
questions.title: MongoDB Performance: `explain()` and Query Optimization
questions.direct_answer: **`explain('executionStats')`** returns the query plan plus runtime metrics — the primary tool for slow-query diagnosis. Look for **`IXSCAN`** (good) vs **`COLLSCAN`** (bad), compare **`totalKeysExamined`** to **`nReturned`** (ratio near 1 is efficient), and watch for in-memory **`SORT`** stages that exceed 100MB. The usual fixes are adding an ESR-compliant compound index, turning a query into a **covered query** (projection + index fully satisfy it), restricting projections, and reducing cardinality early in aggregation pipelines. **Atlas Performance Advisor** and the **database profiler** (`db.setProfilingLevel(1, { slowms: 100 })`) surface which queries to diagnose first.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to use `explain()` end-to-end and translate plan output into actionable index or query changes
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only running `explain()` without `executionStats`, or ignoring the `keys examined / returned` ratio when an index exists but is inefficient
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Walk through a full `executionStats` tree, call out `FETCH` vs `PROJECTION_COVERED`, the 100MB sort limit + `allowDiskUse`, and the ESR rule

sections.title: The Diagnostic Loop
sections.content:
Slow MongoDB queries almost always fall into three buckets: **no suitable index (`COLLSCAN`)**, **index exists but scans too many keys** (bad ordering, missing predicate), or **large in-memory sort** that spills past 100MB.

The workflow is: find the slow query via the **profiler** or **Atlas Performance Advisor**, run **`explain('executionStats')`** to see the plan and runtime stats, and iterate on indexes and query shape until the plan is `IXSCAN` (ideally `PROJECTION_COVERED`) with a key-to-result ratio close to 1.

Two rules drive most index design. **ESR**: Equality → Sort → Range for compound-index field order. **Cover the query** when possible: include every filter, sort, and projected field in the same index so MongoDB never has to fetch the document.

sections.title: Reading `explain('executionStats')`
ESR Rule for Compound Indexes
Covered Queries — Zero FETCH
Profiler, Slow Log, and Atlas Advisor
Aggregation Pipeline Optimizations
sections.content:
**`$match` and `$project` first**

```javascript
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { status: "SHIPPED" } },              // uses { status: 1 } index
  { $project: { customerId: 1, total: 1 } },      // drop unused fields
  { $group: { _id: "$customerId", total: { $sum: "$total" } } }
], { allowDiskUse: true });                        // spill if > 100MB
```

**Additional tips**
- Ensure foreign fields used by `$lookup` are indexed
- Prefer `$merge` / `$out` to materialize expensive results
- Use `$facet` only when necessary — it runs sub-pipelines in parallel but shares the 100MB limit

sections.title: Fix the Right Thing
sections.content:
**When adding an index helps:**
- `COLLSCAN` on a frequent query
- High `totalKeysExamined / nReturned` ratio
- Sort stages that would exceed 100MB

**When adding an index hurts:**
- Write-heavy workloads where every extra index slows writes
- Overlapping indexes (drop older ones after verifying with `$indexStats`)

**Watch for:**
- **Index not being used** — query predicate types don't match (string vs int)
- **`FETCH` after `IXSCAN`** when projection could cover
- **`SORT` stage in plan** — in-memory sort; consider matching index direction
- **`allowDiskUse`** needed for aggregations spilling past 100MB
- **Cached plan staleness** — run `explain('allPlansExecution')` when changes don't seem to help

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`explain('executionStats')`** is the primary diagnostic tool
- **`COLLSCAN` → add index**; **`IXSCAN` with high keys/returned ratio → refine index**
- **ESR rule** for compound-index field ordering
- **Covered queries** eliminate `FETCH` — fastest possible read
- **100MB sort limit**; use `allowDiskUse(true)` for analytics
- **Profiler + Atlas Advisor** surface slow queries to diagnose
- **`$indexStats`** audits usage; drop unused indexes to cut write cost

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Start with the tool**
- `explain('executionStats')` for the plan plus runtime stats
- Look for `IXSCAN` vs `COLLSCAN` and the keys-to-returned ratio

**Apply ESR**
- Equality → Sort → Range for compound-index field order
- Left-prefix rule for derived queries

**Mention covered queries**
- Include every filter, sort, and projected field in the index
- Drop `_id` from the projection
- Plan shows `PROJECTION_COVERED` and `totalDocsExamined: 0`

**Cover the operational tools**
- Profiler `db.setProfilingLevel(1, { slowms: 100 })`
- Atlas Performance Advisor
- `$indexStats` for usage audits

**Close with aggregation tips**
- `$match` first to use indexes
- `allowDiskUse(true)` for > 100MB pipelines
- `$merge` / `$out` for materialized views

questions.question: How do MongoDB replica sets work, and how do read preferences affect how your Spring Boot application reads data?
questions.title: MongoDB Replica Sets and Read Preferences
questions.direct_answer: A **replica set** is a group of `mongod` processes holding the same data — one **primary** accepts all writes, multiple **secondaries** tail the primary's oplog, and an optional **arbiter** votes in elections but stores no data. On primary failure the set **elects** a new primary within ~10s from the members with the most current oplog position. **Read preferences** route reads: `primary` (strong), `primaryPreferred`, `secondary` (offload, may be stale), `secondaryPreferred`, `nearest` (lowest latency). Combined with **`writeConcern: majority`** and **`readConcern: majority`**, you get durable, read-your-writes behavior. In Spring Boot you set the preference on the `MongoClient` connection string or override per `MongoTemplate`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of HA, failover, and the consistency-vs-latency trade-off introduced by secondary reads
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using `readPreference: secondary` for read-your-writes, ignoring replication lag, or using arbiters in production voting critical configurations
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain majority write concern, `maxStalenessSeconds`, election timing, Hidden/Delayed secondary roles, and multi-region read routing

sections.title: Replica Set Fundamentals
sections.content:
A replica set gives you **high availability** and **data redundancy**. The typical shape is three voting members — one primary, two secondaries — on separate hosts and availability zones. **Writes always go to the primary**; secondaries replicate by tailing the primary's **oplog** asynchronously.

When the primary fails, the remaining voting members run an **election**. The secondary with the most current oplog wins, typically within 10–12 seconds. During election writes are rejected with `NotPrimary`; drivers auto-retry once a new primary is elected.

Member roles include **secondary** (replicates, can serve reads), **priority 0** (replicates, cannot become primary — useful for analytics), **hidden** (invisible to drivers; used for backups), **delayed** (holds an intentional lag for point-in-time recovery), and **arbiter** (votes, no data — often discouraged in production because it doesn't increase durability).

sections.title: Replica Set Topology and Read Routing
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    client["Application (driver)"] --> router["Read preference selector"]
    subgraph replicaSet["Replica Set rs0"]
        primary["Primary (writes + strong reads)"]
        sec1["Secondary 1"]
        sec2["Secondary 2"]
        primary -->|"oplog"| sec1
        primary -->|"oplog"| sec2
    end
    router -->|"primary / primaryPreferred"| primary
    router -->|"secondary / secondaryPreferred"| sec1
    router -->|"secondary / secondaryPreferred"| sec2
    router -->|"nearest"| sec1
    router -->|"nearest"| primary
```

sections.title: Read Preference Modes
sections.content:
| Mode | Routes to | Consistency | Typical Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `primary` | Primary only | Strong, read-your-writes | Default; writes + critical reads |
| `primaryPreferred` | Primary, fallback secondary | Strong when possible | HA with graceful fallback |
| `secondary` | Secondaries only | Eventually consistent | Analytics, dashboards |
| `secondaryPreferred` | Secondaries, fallback primary | Eventually consistent | Offload reads |
| `nearest` | Lowest-latency member | May be stale | Geo-distributed, latency-critical reads |

sections.title: Write Concern and Read Concern Recap
sections.content:
**Write concern** — how many replicas ack before success
- `w: 1` — primary only; lost on failover
- `w: "majority"` — durable; standard production default
- `j: true` — fsync journal before ack

**Read concern** — how fresh the read
- `local` — latest on the queried node (may roll back)
- `majority` — only majority-committed data
- `linearizable` — strongest, single-doc only
- `snapshot` — consistent view inside a transaction

**Combine**: `w: majority` + `readConcern: majority` + `readPreference: primary` is the durable read-your-writes default.

sections.title: Configuring Read Preference in Spring Boot
Elections, Lag, and `maxStalenessSeconds`
sections.content:
**Elections**
- Triggered by primary stepping down, network partition, or heartbeat timeout
- Candidate with highest oplog position wins
- Majority of voting members required for quorum
- Writes rejected (`NotPrimary`) during election — drivers retry

**Replication lag**
- Measured via `rs.printSecondaryReplicationInfo()`
- Normal: milliseconds under healthy load
- Can grow to seconds/minutes during replication storms or slow secondaries

**Guard against stale secondary reads**

```java
ReadPreference pref = ReadPreference.secondaryPreferred(
    TagSet.of(),
    60, TimeUnit.SECONDS);  // refuse a secondary > 60s behind
```

`maxStalenessSeconds` forces the driver to skip secondaries that have fallen too far behind.

sections.title: Choosing Preferences Per Workload
sections.content:
**When `primary` helps:**
- Read-your-writes
- Financial, ordering, authoritative reads
- Anywhere stale data is unacceptable

**When `secondary`/`secondaryPreferred` helps:**
- Analytics, dashboards, reports
- Heavy read offload from primary
- Multi-region read latency improvement

**When `nearest` helps:**
- Geo-distributed apps where lowest latency matters more than freshness
- Combined with tagged members for zone-aware routing

**Watch for:**
- **Replication lag** during secondary reads — use `maxStalenessSeconds`
- **Arbiters** don't carry data; avoid them in 3-node production sets — prefer 3 data-bearing nodes
- **Election storms** from flapping networks — tune election timeouts carefully
- **Reading own writes on a secondary** is almost always a bug — stay on primary or use `readConcern: majority` + read-your-writes session tokens

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Replica set = primary + secondaries** replicating async from the oplog
- **Elections** pick a new primary in ~10s from members with the freshest oplog
- **Read preferences** route reads: `primary`, `primaryPreferred`, `secondary`, `secondaryPreferred`, `nearest`
- **`w: majority` + `readConcern: majority`** is the durable read-your-writes default
- **`maxStalenessSeconds`** refuses reads from lagging secondaries
- **Arbiters don't bear data** — avoid in production durability-critical sets
- **Hidden/delayed members** serve backups and point-in-time recovery

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Describe the topology**
- Primary + secondaries + optional arbiter
- Writes to primary, async replication via oplog
- Election in ~10s on primary failure

**Cover read preferences**
- `primary` (default), `primaryPreferred`, `secondary`, `secondaryPreferred`, `nearest`
- Each trades consistency for latency or load offload

**Mention write/read concerns**
- `w: majority` + `readConcern: majority` for durable read-your-writes
- `linearizable` read concern for strict recency (single-doc only)

**Call out gotchas**
- Replication lag on secondaries — use `maxStalenessSeconds`
- Avoid arbiters where durability matters
- Retry `NotPrimary` during elections

**Close with Spring config**
- Connection string or programmatic MongoClient settings
- Per-template beans for analytics (`secondaryPreferred`)
- Per-query overrides when needed

questions.question: How does MongoDB sharding work — shard keys, chunks, the balancer, zones, and `mongos` routing?
questions.title: MongoDB Sharding: Shard Keys, Chunks, Balancer, Zones
questions.direct_answer: MongoDB sharding partitions a collection across shards by the **shard key**. Data is split into **chunks** (default 128MB ranges or hashed buckets); the **balancer** moves chunks between shards to keep distribution even. **`mongos`** routers pull metadata from **config servers** and route each query to the right shard(s) — queries including the shard key are **targeted** (one shard); those without it **scatter-gather** across all shards. **Zones** pin ranges to specific shards for data residency or whale isolation. The shard key choice decides everything — high cardinality, low frequency, non-monotonic (or hashed), query-aligned — and bad choices cause the classic **hot-shard** failure mode that `reshardCollection` (5.0+) fixes online.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Picking a monotonic or low-cardinality shard key, assuming sharding adds free scale without access-pattern discipline
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss `reshardCollection`, hashed vs compound keys, jumbo chunks, zones, targeted vs scatter-gather, and the role of config servers

sections.title: Sharding in One Picture
sections.content:
A sharded MongoDB cluster has three moving parts: **shards** (each a replica set holding a subset of the data), a **config server** replica set (holds cluster metadata — chunks, shard-key ranges, zones), and **`mongos` routers** (stateless query routers in front of the shards).

The **shard key** is a field (or compound of fields) that MongoDB uses to decide which shard owns each document.
- The collection's key range is divided into **chunks** — either 128MB byte ranges (ranged sharding) or evenly-distributed hashed buckets (hashed sharding).
- The **balancer** runs in the background to move chunks between shards when one gets too much data.

**`mongos`** looks up the relevant chunk in the config server, routes the query to the owning shard(s), and merges results. Queries including the shard key are **targeted** (one shard, fast); queries without it **scatter-gather** to all shards (slow, expensive).

sections.title: Sharded Cluster Topology
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    app["Application"] --> mongos1["mongos router 1"]
    app --> mongos2["mongos router 2"]
    mongos1 --> configRs["Config Server Replica Set (metadata)"]
    mongos2 --> configRs
    subgraph shardA["Shard A (replica set)"]
        pa["Primary"] --> sa1["Secondary"]
        pa --> sa2["Secondary"]
    end
    subgraph shardB["Shard B (replica set)"]
        pb["Primary"] --> sb1["Secondary"]
        pb --> sb2["Secondary"]
    end
    subgraph shardC["Shard C (replica set)"]
        pc["Primary"] --> sc1["Secondary"]
        pc --> sc2["Secondary"]
    end
    mongos1 --> pa
    mongos1 --> pb
    mongos1 --> pc
    mongos2 --> pa
    mongos2 --> pb
    mongos2 --> pc
    balancer["Balancer (runs on primary mongos)"] --> configRs
```

sections.title: Enabling Sharding and Picking a Shard Key
Chunks, Balancer, and Routing
Zones for Residency and Whale Isolation
Resharding Online (5.0+)
When Sharding Helps and Hurts
sections.content:
**When it helps:**
- Working set exceeds single-replica-set capacity (> 2TB)
- Sustained writes beyond one replica set (> 20K/s)
- Data residency via zones
- Multi-tenant workloads with whale isolation

**When it hurts:**
- Small datasets — vertical scaling is simpler and cheaper
- Unclear access patterns — shard key becomes structural debt
- Cross-shard queries dominate — scatter-gather everywhere

**Watch for:**
- **Jumbo chunks** — single shard-key value exceeds chunk size; can't split or move
- **Hot shards** — monotonic or whale shard key; fix with `reshardCollection`
- **Scatter-gather queries** — design queries to include the shard key
- **Multi-document transactions across shards** are supported but 2PC-costly
- **Balancer off** — `sh.getBalancerState()` to verify
- **Config server downtime** — cluster becomes read-only for metadata operations

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Cluster = shards + config servers + `mongos`**
- **Shard key** decides per-document shard placement; high cardinality + low frequency + non-monotonic
- **Chunks** are 128MB ranges (ranged) or hashed buckets; **balancer** moves them to keep shards even
- **Targeted queries** include the shard key; **scatter-gather** queries hit every shard
- **Zones** pin ranges to tagged shards — residency, whale isolation, tiered hardware
- **Jumbo chunks** signal a bad shard key
- **`reshardCollection` (5.0+)** changes the shard key online

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Describe the topology**
- Shards (replica sets), config servers, `mongos` routers
- `mongos` is stateless and pulls metadata from config servers

**Explain the shard key**
- Field(s) that decide which shard owns each document
- Good = high cardinality, low frequency, non-monotonic, query-aligned
- Bad = monotonic (ObjectId), low-cardinality, whale values

**Cover chunks and balancer**
- Chunks 128MB ranges or hashed buckets
- Balancer moves chunks to keep distribution even
- Pause per collection during sensitive ops

**Describe routing**
- Targeted query = one shard, fast
- Scatter-gather = every shard, slow — design queries to include the shard key

**Mention zones and resharding**
- Zones pin key ranges to shards for residency or whale isolation
- `reshardCollection` (5.0+) changes the shard key online

**Close with advice**
- Don't shard prematurely — vertical scale goes far
- Test shard distribution with production-scale data before going live
